samples.summary: Attacker-influenced document content can permanently disable the DNS-rebinding address pin for the whole export when an egress proxy is configured
samples.evidence:
`planHop`/`createImageFetcher` claim the pin fallback is "not attacker-triggerable: whether the proxy accepts an address literal is a property of the environment, not of the document" (image-fetcher.ts:512-513). But the trigger is any `SystemError('NETWORK_ERROR')` from `issue(plan)` (line 800-806), and `rawRequest` wraps *every* undici failure into exactly that code (line 662-670) — proxy CONNECT refusal, origin refusal, TLS failure, timeout, unreachable address. The `src` list, its order, and (via a hostile nameserver) the addresses each host resolves to are all chosen by whoever can edit or share the document.

Vector, with `https_proxy`/`http_proxy` set (the only configuration this path exists for): attacker's doc image #1 is `http://a.evil/x`; their nameserver answers the gate's `lookup` with a public-but-unroutable address (e.g. `192.0.2.10`, which `isPrivateAddress` allows). `planHop` rewrites the hop to `192.0.2.10`, the proxy CONNECT/GET to it fails, `rawRequest` raises `NETWORK_ERROR`, and line 808 sets the closure flag `pinThroughProxy = false` **for the remaining lifetime of the fetcher**, then retries image #1 by name — which now succeeds because the proxy resolves `a.evil` itself and the attacker's DNS returns a live host. Image #2 is `http://b.evil/y`: the gate resolves it to a public address and approves, but `planHop(target, addresses, false)` (line 810/787) now hands the *name* to the proxy with no pin, so the proxy performs its own resolution and a ~0s-TTL record can point it at `169.254.169.254` / an internal host on the proxy's network. The fetched bytes are embedded into the exported PDF/DOCX/PPTX the victim reads — precisely the SSRF the pin was added to close.

Secondary aggravator (lower confidence): the pinned-through-proxy path is only exercised in tests over plain `http_proxy` + `http:` origins (test/image-fetcher.test.ts). If undici's `ProxyAgent` does not honour `requestTls.servername` for certificate identity on a CONNECT to an address literal, every `https:` proxied image fails TLS → `NETWORK_ERROR` → the same global downgrade fires on the first HTTPS image, without any attacker involvement.

Minimal hardening: scope the downgrade to the hop that failed (or to a proxy-refusal signal), and never let a document-supplied `src` flip a process-wide security flag.

samples.summary: `assertBrowserInitiated` cannot see the `?mode=cli` cross-site navigation it is documented to refuse — `CliLoginConfirmMiddleware` answers before any guard runs
samples.evidence:
`AuthModule.configure` registers `CliLoginConfirmMiddleware` for `GET auth/github` (auth.module.ts:45-49), and Nest runs middleware strictly before guards — the module's own comment says so ("middleware is the only layer that runs ahead of the guard"). For a cross-site top-level navigation to `/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<attacker's>&nonce=…`, `CliLoginConfirmMiddleware.use` takes the non-`next()` branch (cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:106-113): it sets the confirm cookie and renders the interstitial. `GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate` — and therefore `assertBrowserInitiated` (github-auth.guard.ts:95, 144-155) — is never reached on that request. The guard only ever sees the *second*, same-origin request produced by the Continue click, which reports `same-origin` and is allowed.

So the new check contributes nothing to the CLI shape that docs/design/backend.md and the new `rest-api.md` risk-table row attribute to it ("a hostile page could start a `?mode=cli` round trip in the victim's browser with a loopback port of its choosing"). The real control for that shape remains the confirmation click plus PKCE. The added spec case (`github-auth.guard.spec.ts:186-194`) asserts `{ __cliConfirmed: true, 'sec-fetch-site': 'cross-site' }`, a combination the middleware makes unreachable in production, so the test does not detect the gap. Risk: the risk table now records a control at a layer that cannot enforce it, which is what leads to the real control being removed later as redundant.

samples.summary: `Sec-Fetch-Site` allowlist admits `none` and a missing header, so out-of-band link delivery bypasses the new browser-initiation check
samples.evidence: `assertBrowserInitiated` returns early when the header is absent (line 146) and `ALLOWED_FETCH_SITES` contains `'none'` (line 45). `none` is exactly what a browser sends when the navigation was started by something that is not a page — the OS handler, a native mail/chat client, a desktop app. So the most common real delivery of "a login the user did not start" (a link pasted into email/Slack, or opened by a malicious local program) arrives as `none` and is served, not refused. Older browsers that ship no `Sec-Fetch-*` at all (Safari before 16.4, and anything behind a header-stripping CDN) are likewise served, contradicting the comment's claim that "every browser that can be steered cross-site also sends this" (lines 138-142). `same-site` is also accepted, so a foothold on any sibling subdomain sharing eTLD+1 can initiate a login too. The check therefore only covers a hostile *page* on a different site, in a modern browser, on the non-`mode=cli` path — a narrower guarantee than the docs and risk table state.

samples.summary: No size or time bound on an attacker-chosen image fetch: the export buffers whatever the document's `src` returns
searchedFor: checked planHop/pinnedAgent/makeProxyAgent for undici bodyTimeout or maxResponseSize options
samples.evidence: `return await res.blob()` (line 840) buffers the whole response with no `Content-Length` check, no byte cap and no per-hop `AbortSignal`. The `src` is document content, i.e. chosen by anyone who can edit or share the document, and the gate deliberately permits any public host on any port. A doc whose inline points at a multi-GB endpoint (or a slow-loris endpoint) makes `docs export` / `slides export` allocate until the process is OOM-killed, and a doc with many such inlines multiplies it. The pre-existing code had the same shape, but this change is the one that formalises the fetcher as the trust boundary for attacker-influenced URLs, so the missing resource bound belongs with the rest of the gate.

samples.summary: The security-downgrade flag is published in the agent-facing command schema, contradicting the stated "discoverable only via --help and README" containment
samples.evidence: `--allow-unbound-callback` is added to the machine-readable registry that agents consult to choose flags (registry.ts:48), while docs/design/cli.md states the escape hatch "is documented in `wafflebase login --help` and the CLI README, places an attacker has no say over" and the new lessons doc frames restricted discoverability as part of the mitigation. The registry is not attacker-settable, so this is not the login-fixation vector the design doc worries about, but it does make an automated agent likely to offer/select the flag that disables the callback binding. Worth marking `safety`/deprecated-style in the schema or omitting it.

samples.summary: Unvalidated client-supplied header value is interpolated into a warn-level log line
samples.evidence: `this.logger.warn(\`Refused a cross-site-initiated login (Sec-Fetch-Site: ${value}).\`)` (lines 149-151) logs the raw request header before any vocabulary check. Node's HTTP parser rejects CR/LF in header values, so log-line injection is not reachable, but an arbitrarily long or non-ASCII value is written verbatim to the application log on an unauthenticated endpoint, which is a cheap log-flooding/log-poisoning primitive. Logging a fixed marker (or a truncated, allowlist-checked value) costs nothing.

verdict.reason: The described code exists as claimed. `rawRequest` (image-fetcher.ts:662-670) collapses every undici transport failure into `SystemError('NETWORK_ERROR')`, and the fallback branch (image-fetcher.ts:800-812) triggers on that entire error class, not on a proxy-refusal signal. On the first such failure it sets the fetcher-lifetime closure flag `pinThroughProxy = false` (declared image-fetcher.ts:735, set at 808), after which every later hop plans through `planHop(target, addresses, false)` (787 -> 536-543), which hands the proxy the document-supplied hostname with no address pin, restoring the DNS-rebinding window the pin was added to close — as the fetcher's own warning text admits (740-748). The trigger is attacker-influenced: `src`, its order, and (via a hostile nameserver) the resolved addresses are all document content (the file itself notes documents are attacker-influenced at 71-79), and `isPrivateAddress` permits public-but-unroutable answers such as 192.0.2.10 (105-115), which the repo's own test uses as an address "nothing listens on" (test/image-fetcher.test.ts:719-732). So the comment's claim at 512-513 that the fallback "is not attacker-triggerable" is contradicted by the code path. test/image-fetcher.test.ts:867-902 confirms the downgrade is global for the fetcher (second image never retries the address). The path is reachable from real commands (commands/docs.ts:281, commands/slides.ts:224) with ambient proxy env read by proxyForUrl (603-620). No guard elsewhere prevents the flag flip, and SSRF / weakened security control is in the security lane, so no refutation ground applies.

finding.summary: Reviewer did not produce a valid verdict: review: every credential in the pool (2) was retired — nothing left to fail over to

verdict.reason: The "finding" is not a claim about repository code — it is a verbatim harness failure record. Its prefix is emitted by lensFailureSummary (scripts/agent/review-panel.mjs:1688-1693) and its suffix is the exact string built by poolExhaustedError (scripts/agent/ask.mjs:630-636), where "(2)" is pool.size and "review:" is the lens label. It means the reviewing lens never ran because every credential in its pool was retired (rate-limit window closed or credential refused, per ask.mjs:622-628). It cites no file, no line, and describes no vulnerability: no authorization gate, secret exposure, injection sink, crypto comparison, deserialization, or SSRF. The message itself carries no credential material (only pool.size) and is passed through redactSecrets before publication (review-panel.mjs:1693), with review-panel.mjs:1695-1704 documenting that upstream prose is deliberately never interpolated to avoid exactly the credential-leak class. The one adjacent substantive observation — that a pool-exhausted error lands in the non-infra branch of lensFailureSummary and so renders as a fail-closed blocking finding instead of the infra wire format described at review-panel.mjs:1682-1686 (see rounds.mjs:565 INFRA_SUMMARY) — is a harness classification/correctness matter that errs toward blocking rather than permitting, and is not what this finding asserts. Out of scope for the Security lens rubric.
